title: Decidability with two parametric clocks and arbitrarily many integer parameters
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which always halts and decides finite reachability for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters? For the finite input automaton \(A\), the predicate to decide is \[\exists\mu:P\to\mathbb N\ \exists k\in\mathbb N\ \exists\text{ a legal }k\text{-transition run under }\mu\text{ from }(q_0,\mathbf0)\text{ to }(q_f,v).\] The parameter valuation is chosen once for the whole run; neither its values nor the run length have a supplied bound. Arbitrarily many clocks compared only with numerical constants remain allowed.
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). An input consists of a nonempty finite set of locations \(Q\), an initial location \(q_0\), a target location \(q_f\), a finite set of clocks \(X\), a finite set of parameters \(P\), and a finite list of transitions \((q,g,R,q')\), where \(R\subseteq X\) is a reset set. A guard \(g\) is a finite conjunction of comparisons \(x\bowtie c\) or \(x\bowtie p\), with \(x\in X\), \(c\in\mathbb N\), \(p\in P\) and \(\bowtie\in\{<,\le,=,\ge,>\}\); an empty conjunction is true. At most two distinct clocks occur in any comparison with a parameter anywhere in the automaton. A parametric clock may also be compared with constants. All other clocks may be compared with constants but never with parameters.

A clock valuation is \(v:X\to\mathbb N\), initially zero. For a fixed parameter valuation \(\mu\), a step along \((q,g,R,q')\) chooses a delay \(d\in\mathbb N\), checks \(g\) at the values \(v(x)+d\) with every parameter \(p\) replaced by \(\mu(p)\), and then sets \(v'(x)=0\) for \(x\in R\) and \(v'(x)=v(x)+d\) otherwise. In particular, the guard is tested before the resets, and zero delays are allowed. There are no location invariants, diagonal clock comparisons, parameter arithmetic, clock rates other than one, or resets to values other than zero. A run may stop as soon as its location is \(q_f\); no final clock value is prescribed. A zero-transition run succeeds if \(q_0=q_f\). Since the objective is finite reachability, there is no Büchi, fairness or divergent-time acceptance requirement. All sets and transitions are explicitly listed, numerical constants and indices use binary encodings, and the numbers of parameters and nonparametric clocks are part of the input. The classifier must make an exact yes/no decision on every valid finite description, with no oracle, random error or complexity requirement. The required output is this decision, not a description of every successful parameter valuation.

context_blocks.text: A parametric clock is a clock that is tested against an unknown parameter somewhere in the input. It is not a clock with an unknown rate. All clocks advance together by integer delays, while each parameter is one fixed integer reused at every occurrence during a run.

The source proves EXPSPACE-completeness with two parametric clocks and one parameter. Its proof bounds the size of a successful value for that one parameter. Several independent parameters can constrain the same two clocks in different ways, so the one-parameter theorem does not give the arbitrary-parameter algorithm requested here.

The surrounding boundary is sharp in the number of parametric clocks: one such clock with any finite number of parameters has a decidable, NEXP-complete reachability problem; three parametric clocks already make reachability undecidable, even with one parameter. The source states these results for the integer-time setting.

The saved card permits conjunctions of simple guards, whereas the source’s elementary transition presentation uses one comparison per edge. Conjunctions can be checked along a finite sequence with no intervening time elapse, enforced by an extra nonparametric clock. This does not increase the number of parametric clocks, which is the constrained resource; the more readable conjunction presentation is retained.

Integer-valued parameters do not by themselves mean integer time: another model lets clocks take arbitrary real values. Digitization transfers certain closed-guard cases, but this card includes strict comparisons and explicitly uses discrete time. It does not silently identify all dense-time variants with its target.

The March 2025 draft with a similar title considers an infinite-word Büchi problem, real-valued time and parameters, one parameter, and a restriction forbidding a clock from being tested and reset on the same edge. Its positive claim therefore does not resolve unrestricted-parameter finite reachability in this model.

why: Timing parameters turn verification of a fixed timed system into the search for a working assignment of unknown delays and deadlines. With one parametric clock reachability is decidable, while three parametric clocks already yield undecidability. The two-clock case with unrestricted parameter count is a precise boundary between these behaviors, with connections to counter machines and arithmetic with divisibility.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for exactly this input class. A positive result must specify one total computable classifier and prove equivalence with existence of a fixed nonnegative integer parameter valuation and a finite legal run. A negative result must prove that no such classifier exists with at most two parametric clocks; adding a third such clock does not settle the target. A procedure that enumerates only successful valuations, a theorem for a fixed bound on the number of parameters, or an algorithm that may diverge on negative instances is insufficient. Dense-time or infinite-word results require a proved reduction preserving every model restriction before they can be used.

progress.text: The source traces the model and the one-versus-three parametric-clock decidability boundary to Alur, Henzinger and Vardi.
The STACS theorem proves EXPSPACE-completeness for two parametric clocks and one parameter, while retaining the unrestricted parameter count as open.
The journal version is published online; it explicitly retains arbitrary numbers of nonparametric clocks and parameters as the unresolved two-parametric-clock case. The issue date is August 2024.
The checked draft studies a restricted real-time Büchi variant with one parameter; its acceptance, time and reset conventions differ from this target.
The integer-valued clock and parameter conventions, guard/reset order and source boundary theorems were checked; bounded later-primary searches found no matching resolution.

status_note: Explicitly open in the Göller–Hilaire STACS 2021 paper and its journal version published online 24 April 2023 (Theory of Computing Systems 68, 2024). Their EXPSPACE-completeness theorem fixes one parameter, while the target allows arbitrarily many. The March 2025 non-resetting-test draft has different time, parameter and infinite-word conventions. Bounded later-work checking on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this does not certify absence of every later result.

sentences: A discrete-time parametric timed automaton compares integer-valued clocks with constants and with unknown nonnegative integer parameters.
The question asks whether some fixed assignment of all parameters allows a finite run to a designated target location.
Only two clocks may be compared with parameters, but both the number of parameters and the number of other clocks are unrestricted.
The one-parameter case is EXPSPACE-complete, while nearby real-time infinite-word results do not settle this arbitrary-parameter reachability question.
A resolution would close the central two-parametric-clock gap between known decidable and undecidable timing models.
